content: Fluoride compounds, like most substances, are toxic when present in high concentrations. Ingesting 5 grams of pure sodium fluoride is lethal for most adults, with the estimated lethal dose being approximately 70 mg per kilogram of body weight. Acute fluoride toxicity is believed to occur at doses ranging from 2 to 8 mg per kilogram of body weight, with lethal doses reported at 16 mg/kg in children and 32-64 mg/kg in adults. Poisoning typically results from accidental or intentional ingestion of fluoride-containing products. When ingested, fluoride compounds are rapidly absorbed through the intestines. Over time, they are excreted via the urine, with a half-life of several hours. The body removes fluoride from circulation, with trace amounts being deposited in bone. Urine tests are effective in detecting recent high exposure to fluoride compounds. Contact with fluoride compounds at high concentrations, whether through the skin or eyes, is hazardous. The only widely recognized adverse effect of low-concentration water fluoridation is dental fluorosis. This condition arises from excessive fluoride intake during tooth development (before teeth erupt into the mouth) and can result in tooth discoloration (yellowing), hypothyroidism, or increased brittleness of bones and teeth. Fluoridated water is recommended at levels of 2 ppm. In small amounts, fluoride is beneficial for dental health (see fluoride therapy). However, fluoride toxicity can cause gastrointestinal inflammation due to its corrosive effects on the mucous membranes lining the gut. Fluoride toxicity may also exacerbate the effects of natural plant toxins, such as salicylates. This is particularly significant in subgroups with a high prevalence of salicylate intolerance, such as individuals with ADHD or autism (see autism therapies). Possible Sources of Fluoride Poisoning Fluoride poisoning can result from various sources, though not all have been scientifically proven as direct causes. Historically, most cases have been linked to accidental ingestion of insecticides or rodenticides. Potential sources include: Air pollution Anesthetics Antibiotics Automobile wheel-cleaning products Contaminated beverages and food products Dietary supplements containing sodium fluoride Fluoridated milk Fluoridated salt Fluoridation of public water supplies Fluoride tablets Glass-etching or chrome-cleaning agents (e.g., ammonium bifluoride) Groundwater pollution Household products Industrial exposure to fluxes used in metal processing Insecticides containing sodium fluoride Mattresses emitting fluoride gases Scotchgard Soy products Rodenticides containing sodium fluoride Tea Teflon Toothpaste or other dental products containing sodium monofluorophosphate Vaccine contamination Chronic Toxicity This article primarily addresses acute fluoride toxicity, which results from ingesting a large amount of fluoride in a short period. Chronic toxicity, on the other hand, occurs from prolonged ingestion of small amounts of fluoride. Chronic exposure can lead to dental fluorosis and skeletal fluorosis, conditions observed in regions where natural fluoride levels in drinking water exceed those added to public water supplies in the United States. Symptoms of Acute Toxicity Acute fluoride toxicity manifests through a range of symptoms, often appearing within minutes of exposure. The severity of symptoms depends on the amount of fluoride ingested. These symptoms suggest significant metabolic dysfunction, resembling those seen in hypothyroidism. Gastrointestinal Symptoms Abdominal pain Diarrhea Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) Hypersalivation Mucosal injury Nausea Vomiting Electrolyte Abnormalities Hyperkalemia (elevated potassium levels) Hypocalcemia (low calcium levels) Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar levels) Hypomagnesemia (low magnesium levels) Neurologic Effects Headache Hyperactive reflexes Muscle weakness Muscular spasms Paresthesia (tingling or numbness) Seizures Tetanic contractions Tremors Cardiovascular Effects Cardiac arrest Shock Widening of the QRS complex on an electrocardiogram Various arrhythmias Mechanism of Action Ingested fluoride primarily acts on the intestinal mucosa. In the stomach, it can form hydrofluoric acid, which causes irritation or corrosion of the gastrointestinal lining. The gastrointestinal tract is the first and most commonly affected organ system following fluoride ingestion. Treatment In cases of accidental ingestion, administering milk, calcium carbonate, or milk of magnesia can help slow fluoride absorption. For skin or eye contact, contaminated clothing should be removed, and the affected area should be thoroughly flushed with water.
